An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle distribution patterns, specifically for light mesons like pions and kaons within the Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC operating at 5.02 TeV. Fluctuations of the $\Psi_n$ angle are observed to behave in the same way across different collision centralities, and are found to be comparable in magnitude to those observed in the ALICE experiment at a collision energy of 2.76 TeV. Furthermore, the ratio of fluctuations in the $v_n$ magnitude to the average $v_n$ magnitude is found to be highest at the lowest collision centrality examined, with an observed trend that fluctuations in the $v_n$ magnitude are more significant for higher harmonic patterns (e.g. $v_4$ vs $v_2$). These findings are in line with theoretical predictions made through the Wigner semi-circle distribution, and are also compared to the ALICE experiment's earlier findings at the 2.76 TeV collision energy.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to four distinct contexts of data quality evaluations.

This study introduces TV-PAR, a novel flexible dynamic model consisting of a changing autoregressive component and a time-varying intensity parameter for count time series data. Unlike traditional PAR models that assume parameter stability and offer parametric estimates, the TV-PAR model utilizes trigonometric smoothing regression to model non-parametric time-varying parameters, allowing for changes in the intensity parameter across time. We derive an asymptotically unbiased estimator for the intensity parameter and demonstrate consistency and a delta-method-based asymptotic distribution for the estimator. Furthermore, we prove the asymptotic efficiency of the estimator under certain conditions, including a delta-method-based asymptotic distribution. Simulated examples illustrate the performance of TV-PAR, and a real-data analysis applies the model to a dataset featuring football goal counts.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating successful past actions on similar objects. To achieve
this, we use a query network to generate NDFs for a target object, and a plan
network to produce a possible action plan based on these descriptors. We train
both networks jointly, with the plan network's predictions being used to guide
the training on the manipulation dataset. Our method excels at repeating past
actions on novel objects of the same category, with results surpassing current
state-of-the-art in object manipulation by a significant margin. With the use
of 3D descriptors, NDFs also outperform previous representations on object
recognition tasks.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.68 for N=1, 1.70 for N=2, and 1.69 for N>=3. These values supersede previous estimates obtained with the one-loop long-wavelength renormalization expansion.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, we used this inequality to demonstrate the efficacy of a biased random walk algorithm in efficiently exploring the set of pure Nash equilibria, as predicted by a conjecture known as the Sudakov-Fernique conjecture.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps as intermediate cues in the first stage. Subsequent construction of correspondence constraints is achieved via learning a correspondence network utilizing these heatmaps in the second stage. The proposed framework is referred to as DeepHMap++. The proposed architecture is particularly suitable for challenging scenarios featuring partial occlusion, rich background, and limited textural information. The efficacy of DeepHMap++ is demonstrated through extensive experiments on three widely used datasets: the LMO-360 dataset, the airway tube dataset, and the LIDAR-based household furniture dataset. The results show that DeepHMap++ delivers superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art patch-based methods and the majority of two-stage pipelines.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, has exhibited impressive multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough with dark excitons has been achieved without the use of a external magnetic field, overcoming a previous limitation.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from the non-symmorphic wallpaper group, utilizing a 2D silicon carbide surface root lattice as a physical reference point. By applying a certain misorientation angle to $\theta$ and matching it with a specific superlattice spacing along the $x$-axis as $\Delta/a_0 = 2\sqrt{3}$, we create a honeycomb-like lattice with an "ortho-hexagonal" symmetry from the NS$6$ lattice type. Through a combination of tight-binding models and a $k\cdot p$ method, we've identified non-symmorphic wallpaper group physics which exhibit both topological and ortho-hexagonal symmetry. As a result, this leads to the creation of a Dirac cone's double point, both of which can be dynamically altered through either magnetic fields or strain within the lattice structure. This results in either the opening or the collapse of a band gap around the double Dirac point, which can range from approximately 1eV to nearly 6eV in the lattice structure.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with minimal reliance on external information sources. To achieve this, we developed an automatic, densely connected Unet called DDAUnet that employs both channel and spatial attention mechanisms to prioritize relevant image features for better tumor boundary predictions. To validate our method, we conducted experiments on two separate datasets containing pre-annotated CT scans of tumors in the esophagus, yielding DDAUnet's state-of-the-art performance according to segmentation accuracy metrics.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years, incorporating a measure of geographical sorting based on census data. The results reveal that in more intensely sorted regions, misleading information about COVID-19 and election-related topics was more widely shared on Reddit. Furthermore, we found that users from highly sorted areas were more likely to engage with untruthful content, although this behavior could be explained by existing personality traits or psychological variables. In contrast, we found no direct link between geographical sorting and users' willingness to believe in misinformation. Our findings suggest that the Big Sort contributes to the spread of online misinformation by increasing the social cohesion of sorted communities and fostering a sense of trust among its members. This trust in turn enables misinformation to gain traction within these communities.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not account for the significance of auditory feedback from the instructor. To enhance robotic learning through demonstration and observation, it is crucial to investigate the impact of auditory feedback from human teachers during task demonstrations. This study examines how audio patterns emitted by humans while demonstrating manipulation tasks to robots are influenced by factors such as their own physical ability to perform the task, the level of clarity in their instructions, and the level of difficulty associated with the task being demonstrated to them. The research involves participants performing manipulation tasks in front of a robot while providing verbal instructions, with varying levels of physical ability and task difficulty. The resulting audio patterns are analyzed to determine their impact on future task demonstrations. The study's findings suggest that individuals with greater manual dexterity tend to demonstrate tasks more quickly, whereas those with lesser dexterity struggle with more complex tasks, leading to slower demonstration speeds. Furthermore, this research provides a framework for classifying audio feedback into four distinct categories: initial task instruction, hand movement sounds during demonstration, pause sounds indicating mistakes, and concluding task instruction. These findings and audio pattern classifications are expected to aid in the development of more effective methods for teaching robots new skills through demonstration and observation, taking into account the influence of auditory feedback from the human teacher.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity minimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into the diverse equations that serve as conformal field theory complexity optimality conditions and systematically examining their inherent properties. Notably, we derive the Euler-Arnold equation as the specific ideal case, and demonstrate that it adheres to the golden ratio π/2ΔxΔt in both the high-precision relativistic regime and the corresponding semi-relativistic regime characterized by a small Δx/Δt ratio. All derived results are physically interpretable, offering insights into the Fubini-Study metric's behavior as well as its underlying connection to the geometric mean state or operator complexity.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple fronts using publicly available data sets, incorporating feedback from radiology professionals to enhance image characterization. Analyzing across different research sites, MRI scan purposes were found difficult to predict, but attributes of individual images could be accurately classified, and the pipeline's ability to distinguish between usable and unusable data was consistently demonstrated across various datasets, albeit with a notable limitation in accurately identifying unusable data in certain samples. Further research is required to improve predictive modeling of MRI scan objectives. In addition to its utility in research, this study also highlights practical applications of MRI data preprocessing and characterization in clinical radiology settings.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we've constrained the average matter density of the universe, $\Omega_m$, finding $\Omega_m = 0.57^{0.10}_{0.11}$, and the effect of weak lensing on SN Ia distances has been accounted for as a lensing-induced shift of magnitudes, with a standard deviation of 0.154. This estimation of the Pantheon SN Ia dataset falls within the range of previous estimates from the SNLS3 and SDSS combined with the Hubble Space Telescope F415W and W-MMT data sets.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Typically, a detector is evaluated based on its accuracy in identifying the
presence of objects within an image, without regard to its visual context.
In contrast, we examine the context's impact on object detection by using
a novel dataset that includes both images and context descriptions.
To demonstrate the significance of context, we analyze detection results
from leading deep object detectors using a metric that accounts for the
provided context.
Our study reveals that, despite their high overall performance, these
detectors struggle with certain instances where the context is crucial for
accurate detection.
To illustrate this difficulty, an example is provided where the context
between two objects is essential for determining their class.
Our findings suggest that context within images poses a greater challenge
for current object detectors than extrinsic context, implying that many
detection failures result from the lack of essential visual information rather
than external factors.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are nonhomogeneous, given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type for functions of binary random variables, surpassing previous results by achieving tighter concentrations when functions exhibit little dependence on a large portion of the variables. For the SCP that includes declining associations as a special case, our inequalities regarding functions of binary random variables are sharper than the log-Sobolev inequality-based bounds obtained in [B. J. J. Kim, arXiv 2019]. For functions defined over binary random variables from distributions satisfying SRP, our estimates outperform the existing bounds derived in [B. J. J. Kim, arXiv 2019] under weak uniform mixing and extend the results in [D. C. Stein, Ann. Probab. 2005] to functions of all dependencies, not just independent variables.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.
Numerical simulations are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound for learning CCE, providing support for the associated scalability boundary.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of branching with over 8 possible responses for 
each history. We've designed the MultiTalk Challenge to engage the machine 
learning community in addressing several crucial dialogue tasks. For the first 
task, participants must predict one out of five possible response options for 
a given dialogue history. For the second task, they must rank a set of response 
options for a particular dialogue scenario. We've established two evaluation 
metrics: the first is a simple accuracy for the first task and the second, the 
average AUC-ROC for ranking response options in the second task. With the 
introduction of MultiTalk, we aim to address several key challenges in dialogue 
generation such as controlling topics, maintaining coherence through consecutive 
turns, selecting appropriate response lengths, and incorporating explicit user 
preferences into the model.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program is capable of producing high-resolution N-body simulations, incorporating the effects of modified gravity, and is designed to meet the demands of large-scale cosmological projections requiring numerous simulations. MG-GLAM includes initial condition generation and is compatible with the public ATKaMBA code for N-body simulations. It specifically supports the development of modified gravity models, such as $f(R)$ gravity, where the relation between the Hubble parameter and the scale factor is modified. This tool also enables the generation of N-body simulations for the $\Lambda$CDM model, a well-studied cosmological theory. We validate MG-GLAM by creating N-body simulations for the $f(R)$ gravity and $\Lambda$CDM models, using a high-performance computing framework. These simulations can be utilized as input for semi-analytical models of galaxy formations and evolution. MG-GLAM is an open-source platform, and its capabilities are demonstrated through a series of N-body simulations available online.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the upper half-plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal invariance. Specifically, they considered pairs consisting of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{H}$ and a $\mathbb{D}$-valued field $f_\Omega$ for which $f_\Omega \circ \Phi^{-1} \in \mathcal{H}^2(\mathbb{D})$ for the Riemann map $\Phi$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{D}$. Our work builds upon this idea by defining an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the upper half-plane and associated Cho-Anderson stochastic log-gas, which is equivalent to pairs consisting of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{H}$ and a $\mathbb{D}$-valued field $f_\Omega$ for which $f_\Omega \circ \Phi^{-1} \in \mathcal{H}^2(\mathbb{D})$ for the conformal mapping $\Phi$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb{D}$. We prove that for any such pairing, multiple independent chordal SLE$(\kappa_1, \kappa_2, \mu_1, \mu_2)$ curves driven by the Cho-Anderson stochastic log-gas intersecting the real line and lying within $\mathbb{H}$

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration. The underlying architecture of
WorkingWiki is highly modular and extensible, allowing users to customize its
behavior through 'extensions' – reusable modules of code that can be easily
interchanged for different applications. As proof of its versatility, WorkingWiki
is presented here as an example of its own development, showcasing the power of
which the community can harness this technology for their own purposes.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging for many existing models. However, by using LES-RANS hybrid models, it is possible to achieve this goal. The work's results demonstrate a notable agreement with previous studies that used other methods to model the same jet flame. Furthermore, it highlights the advantages of using LES-RANS models in analyzing sub-flame-length scales of jet flames.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 \nu \beta \beta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective mass would have difficulty detecting a signal.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on how association signals across the genome correlate with specific traits, and we've applied this method to 18 human traits across 12 different annotation types. Our analysis shows that certain annotations, such as regions near gene promoters, are more frequently associated with traits than others, and we've established a hierarchy of annotations by comparing their associations with a random forest algorithm. Notably, our results highlight significant connections between certain annotations and traits that prior studies had missed, and we've made the annotation hierarchy and associated predictions available for further use.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling and measuring quantum interactions at the chemical bond level.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI models' outputs with the majority voting technique yields the most accurate results. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure known as Diversity Augmentation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in a 22% improvement in NLI Diversity. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ghritli/SDNLI.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model rotating stars with masses similar to red dwarfs and radii up to 1.7 times larger than typical red dwarfs, and provided insights that could be used to study sub-stellar objects, including exoplanets and brown dwarfs, by relating simulated results to observed physical characteristics.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctutations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
kinematic regions. This article presents an analytical approach to incorporating 
efficiency and background information into amplitude analyses, specifically for the 
case of two-particle final states with one massive particle. This method involves 
minimizing a chi-squared function that represents discrepancies between actual and 
predicted efficiency and background patterns. As a result, this technique can derive 
the complex coefficients of a likelihood function that, when maximized, yields the 
best-fit parameters and amplitude polynomials. This methodology is particularly 
suitable for modern computing capabilities and can be applied to various analyses, 
including those with varying background levels and efficiency patterns over kinematic 
regions. Additionally, this method has been applied to the analysis of $B^+\to D_k^{(*)+}
  \mu^+ \nu_\mu$, which involves a complex relativistic decay chain with the $D_k^{(*)+}
  \to K^+ K_s \pi^+$ final state.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components. This new paradigm successfully bridges the gaps between various afterglow scenarios by incorporating radiative and adiabatic phases within a singular framework. By taking into account various afterglow environments, this model can be applied to predict afterglow observations across a wide range of situations, from gamma-ray bursts with flat or peaked spectra to fireballs in multiple external media. This new paradigm also provides explicit constraints on key afterglow variables, including the peak frequencies of radiated emissions, flux densities, and radiated energies, which can be derived from observable signatures through radiative analysis of afterglow dynamics.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a model that includes actuator dynamics and use it to develop a control strategy based on reference trajectories, feedforward and feedback components. By applying the chain method, we will derive the derivatives of the reference trajectories and ensure that the feedback component meets the performance criteria. As a result, we will demonstrate that performance standards are met across the entire gait cycle. To validate our approach, we will apply it to a hypothetical robot with thrusters in its legs.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series.

To counter side-channel attacks via Spectre variant 1, the default mitigation strategy involves adding delays to CPU executions and switching data caches. However, by exploiting these precautions, the efficiency of modern computing systems can significantly decline. To rectify this issue, we propose an alternative security-enhanced technique called HyperDegrade, which aims to achieve comparable protection efficiency of the original delay-based method but with significantly reduced computational overhead. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade yields an average 23% performance improvement and 17% energy consumption reduction for various workloads on x86-64 CPUs. Moreover, we discover that introducing only partial L3 cache exclusion is sufficient to achieve the same security level as full L3 cache exclusion, resulting in a 4% performance boost for certain workloads with minimal energy consumption impacts. Our research into general L3 cache exclusion guidelines provides actionable advice for optimizing system efficiency without compromising security.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram is capable of being transformed into an unknotted state using a sequence of four localized operations, as shown by Joel Hass, Robert Kleinberg, and Matthew Tisick's previous work. This research delivers two novel unknotting operations: a classical one for diagrammatic representation and a corresponding operation for welded knots. The newly introduced classical operation is more straightforward than its predecessor, utilizing two localized swatches instead of four, whereas the corresponding operation for welded knots employs five localized swatches. As proof for these new operations, the researchers draw upon an all-encompassing, systematic analysis of possible local modifications, which they refer to as the "unlinking machine." This machine, in turn, is comprised of a vast array of local operators that can be combined to create various unknotting sequences for any given knot.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we derive our cocycle, I(X), through the use of graph-based configuration space integrals rather than combinatorial approaches used by Mortier.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.
