We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, for code rates less than half, we demonstrate the efficacy of the maximum-likelihood decoding algorithm in correcting symmetric errors of any desired rank, provided the error matrix's trace exceeds a certain threshold that decreases proportionally with the desired error rank. Secondly, for code rates greater than half, the same algorithm can correct symmetric errors of any desired rank, under the condition that the error matrix's trace exceeds a threshold that increases proportionally to the square of the desired error rank. Both of these findings improve upon existing maximum-likelihood decoding capabilities for rate-ratio less than one.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 540 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio of approximately 0.25 in SN~2020jfo, and found this ratio to be higher than average for low-luminosity SNe~II and similar to average for high-luminosity SNe~II. Models suggest that SN~2020jfo resulted from a 13 solar mass progenitor star with a metallicity of at least one third of solar masses, and that its small plateau duration could be attributed to a relatively fast luminosity evolution during the hydrogen recombination phase.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, the model's performance eventually declined, indicating a limit to its predictive capabilities.

We have developed a new numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to pinpoint the most questionable model predictions that require additional information. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which are expected to abound. As such, there's a growing interest in developing efficient methods for distinguishing between these mergers through analysis of gravitational waves. By employing a feature extraction method and a neural network, we've created a 6-component model that accurately differentiates between the mergers of black holes and neutron stars. Our results show that this model can successfully distinguish between these mergers with a 94% accuracy level. Furthermore, by incorporating a new method for automatically extracting features from time-domain signals, we've observed no decline in the predictive performance of the model. This finding's implications are significant, as they suggest that, with sufficient training, neural networks are capable of accurately differentiating between the mergers of compact binaries solely on the basis of their gravitational wave signals, a discovery with substantial consequences for the collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects, which then orbit the central star for a significant period. This phenomenon is likely common among developing high-mass stars and can be crucial for their growth, as well as the formation of intermediate-mass black holes through the accumulation of these objects over time. By applying these findings to a sample of observed X-ray binaries containing a stellar companion, we find that mergers between objects in the disk could result in Luminous X-ray Binaries, and that a substantial number of black holes, including intermediate-mass ones, may have been formed through the accumulation of these objects in the disks of high-mass young stellar objects.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation context, specifically when the flow has a constant vorticity. To begin, we review the relevant physics and mathematical formulations before deriving the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation for this particular scenario of water waves. The derived Hamiltonian Dysthe equation is then analyzed to understand its underlying properties, including how energy is preserved and how the wave spectrum evolves over time. The study also compares the obtained results with previously proposed similar equations, offering insights into their limitations and valid applicability ranges. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation predictions are further validated through numerical simulations of wave evolution in both the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) and the modulational instability cases. The research findings related to the energy conservation and the evolution of the wave spectrum are specifically analyzed in the context of the KdV case, while the modulational instability is studied in the context of the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, and both cases are compared with previous research proposals. The research into constant vorticity water waves may serve as a foundation for exploring more complex shear flow cases.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. To address this issue, a novel method has been developed for the navigation of indoor environments using a layered control system and a mobile robot equipped with sonar sensors. The approach involves dividing the navigation process into two distinct levels: a high-level controller responsible for defining a suitable search area within the environment, and a lower-level controller that manages the sonar sensors to obtain a 2D map of the surrounding space. The novel aspect of this approach lies in its capacity to combine real-time sonar data in a manner that prioritizes both local obstacle avoidance and efficient route discovery. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated through a series of simulation and actual experiments conducted in various indoor settings.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media platforms have made it effortless for anyone to become a journalist, but the lack of accountability from these same platforms for publishing unverified information has led to widespread dissemination of false news. This form of false information has been linked to various consequences, including influencing political outcomes and causing financial losses. As a result of its growing impact, researchers have been working diligently to develop methods to identify false news, leveraging AI and machine learning techniques. In this research, we explore the use of pre-trained language models for unsupervised false news detection on Reddit forums. In addition to evaluating these models, we also assess the efficacy of their abstract-generated summaries in differentiating true from false news content. Our analysis reveals that, despite being simply a secondary analysis of our primary experiment, comparing the summary-generated features using a statistical test can offer valuable insights into the performance of LLMs. To this end, we are releasing our code and dataset for further research into LLM-based unsupervised false news detection and summary-generated embeddings.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem function up to a constant value. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow speed. In response to this limitation, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The development of HiTMap is demonstrated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration on an AGV.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Furthermore, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that represents the distribution of each component, allowing us for inference through the use of the barycenter of the prior, which can be efficiently computed.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access for sparse and irregular data structures.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including natural language processing, graph-based algorithms, and mathematical solvers, could significantly benefit from object-oriented programming on SIMD devices.  To address this gap, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel object-oriented programming framework for SIMD devices that features a high-performance memory allocator and optimized memory access techniques.  Compared to existing object-oriented programming solutions for SIMD devices, DynaSOAr's memory allocator uses a fully dynamic and separate memory allocation approach that outperforms existing solutions by up to 2.5 times and offers better memory utilization.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's memory access techniques, which are designed to minimize cache conflicts and enable efficient memory coalescing, result in memory access patterns that are up to 1.8 times more efficient than existing solutions.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. For the Mn dimer, varying inter-atomic distances were examined, and the transition from a double well to a coupled well behavior was characterized by analyzing the spatial distribution of the YSR states. A notable discrepancy between the theoretical and experimental results for the magnetic field-induced shift of the YSR hole state suggested the presence of an intrinsic mechanism affecting the YSR states. Moreover, an assumption of a fixed magnetic moment magnitude was made, although magnetic order on the Nb(110) surface might necessitate further investigation.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions.

We employed density-functional theory to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile titanium dioxide.  Calculations using both generalized gradient approximation and screened hybrid DFT methods were performed to accurately capture the localized and delocalized electron behavior.  Our results indicate that both carbon and nitrogen can give rise to localized magnetic moments in rutile TiO2, with nitrogen exhibiting higher magnetic stability.  The absence of experimental evidence for nitrogen's magnetic signal may be attributed to small cluster size limitations in measurements.  To induce magnetism in TiO2, we found that N 2p-Ti 3d pi-bonding formation is crucial, with associated orbital occupations critical for determining the system's collinearity.  The small energy gap between the conduction band and the high-spin state in N-doped TiO2 suggests that this system may exhibit both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic behavior under different charge states.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data at the CERN LHC, with the hope that this could be a significant signal for new physics beyond the Standard Model. I also outline the potential for the Large Hadron Collider to upgrade its capabilities to directly produce highly elastic scattering patterns, effectively turning the Large Hadron Collider into a giant "elastic scattering machine".

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through the interaction of high-power lasers with solid materials, specifically within the context of QED effects. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses, particularly in particle physics research that requires highly polarized positrons. A theoretical study presents the notion that despite the tiny size of polarized effects, they could have a significant impact when considering the polarization of positrons emitted at certain angles, potentially leading to a detectable signal with sufficient statistical analysis. In particular, the potential for a highly polarized positron source is envisioned, utilizing a thin, non-magnetic material target with high density and low atomic number, to maximize polarization effects while minimizing energy loss due to heat and electron-positron pair creation. The proposed research aims to validate the predicted degree of polarization (expected to be over 70%) through the production of dense, highly polarized positrons, primarily of the low-energy variety, with the long-term goal of leveraging this source in particle physics research that requires intense, high-polarization positrons, possibly replacing magnetic particle accelerators. The feasibility of this research will be explored through the performance of 3D numerical simulations of the interaction between a high-power laser and a foil target, as well as the development of an analytical framework for predicting the polarization properties of produced positrons. The outcome has the potential to open up new possibilities in particle physics research, with applications in the fields of condensed matter and high-energy

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result from group theory and provides a more detailed understanding of how groups are structured.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, reducing the overall circuitry and minimizing power losses. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 25 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C.

We establish a framework for various geometric structures on Lie groupoids in the context of smooth manifold theory and its extension to differential stacks. This framework is then used to define key concepts such as connections, metrics, and Dirac operators on the orbit space of a Lie groupoid, with relevant invariance properties. The development relies on the principle of minimizing the requirement for underlying manifold theoretic objects to include differential stacks. As a result, we derive a definition of differential stacks as a foundation for geometric objects that are invariant under smooth transformations.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research into the mass function of prestellar cores within the Dragon cloud is necessary to fully understand the development of massive star formation.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric and asymmetric, are presented in this study. The results obtained through computation are matched against a set of approximate equations derived from a stability analysis of the membrane's behavior, which includes both its curvature and tension-driven restorative forces in a nonlinear response to the inflicted strain. This matching is particularly evident in areas surrounding the primary bifurcation point. However, a discrepancy is observed near the inner wall of the cell, where the exact analysis overestimates the size of the developed finger. Notably, the results obtained for an inextensible membrane align with those of previous studies, which were obtained through a stability analysis of the cell's inner wall. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH to CN ratio for cyclopentadiene is approximately 3.5, whereas for benzene it is around 0.3. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter's equation, which yields results when plotted against various parameters. These plots demonstrate the model's ability to replicate observed Hubble parameter values by smoothly transitioning between two known cosmological eras. A dimensionless age-shuffle diagnostic tool is introduced to analyze the model's age-of-the-universe predictions. This diagnostic's results are correlated with the current Hubble ratio and indicate that the model's age is influenced by the deceleration parameter. In turn, this dependence on the deceleration parameter is linked to the model's cosmological parameters, which can be determined through a dimensionless combination of the density and pressure at the present epoch. A dimensionless entropy density plot is introduced as a third diagnostic tool. These diagnostics enable the model to replicate key observed cosmological characteristics by smoothly transitioning between two distinct eras, supported by numerical computations of the model's age and entropy density.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino and dark matter interactions. We studied three types of neutrino interactions (S, P, V/A) and three types of dark matter interactions (magnetic moment, scalar and pseudoscalar). We determined the upper limits for neutrino and dark matter production cross-sections based on J/ψ decay into visible photons accompanied by invisible matter. These limits were obtained using a Lorentz structure fit for J/ψ decay into visible photons with missing energy. We found upper limits on neutrino and dark matter production cross-sections for various interactions and at different J/ψ energy levels. These results can be compared with other J/ψ production processes and are expected to aid in interpreting similar experiments in the future.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. The benefits of MFSSA become particularly evident when working with complex data sets that MFSA is unable to adequately handle.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, a novel approach has been developed, known as W-Net, which is designed to automatically segment cell nuclei by leveraging image inpainting. This model utilizes two consecutive convolutional networks, where the second network generates the mask used in the inpainting process, and the first network is utilized for actual cell nucleus detection. Evaluations using two separate datasets have demonstrated that W-Net outperforms existing competing methods in terms of both detection accuracy and the corresponding masks. The developed model is particularly efficient at handling difficult-to-detect nuclei, and the code is available for public use.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic if the underlying fields of their realization as infinite matrix groups are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of the supercuspidal representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by T. Cai and the coauthor for the cases of even dimensional groups.

Deep Neural Network structures like Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), especially those using fully connected layers, are difficult for researchers to understand due to their complex, opaque nature.  GCNNs that work with separate layers for each node in a data graph often result in better performance, but these come with a higher computational cost and are even harder to analyze.  This research focuses on exploring the fundamental workings of graph convolutional layers within GCNNs and provides a simple, transparent variant called MFFNet, which demonstrates a way to reduce the level of node-specific complexity without sacrificing performance.  Through experiments on six well-known datasets, MFFNet achieves performance on par with the current state of the art.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are second-order differential equations for the gauge field, depending on its own derivative, the Weyl tensor, and the conformally invariant Laplacian of the scalar field. The system's properties are then analyzed for both black hole and soliton configurations, concluding that they can evolve under certain external influences such as electromagnetic fields, due to the theory's stability, and that the soliton solutions can be described as conformally flat with a constant scalar field, depending on specific parameters of the underlying symmetry.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties, specifically lateral displacement, is crucial for distinguishing benign and malignant tissues. The quality of estimated parameters, however, is heavily influenced by the spatial resolution of the imaging array, which is a major limitation given the low spatial resolution of many ultrasound elastography techniques. This restriction can be bypassed by the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method, which enhances the spatial resolution through the estimation of lateral displacement at the image formation stage rather than the estimation stage. Our research involves the development and assessment of VSSA for the precise estimation of lateral displacement in elastography. The resulting algorithm was tested on numerical simulations and real-world data, yielding notable improvements in both the spatial resolution and the accuracy of estimated parameters. The results demonstrate the VSSA method to be an efficient and accurate solution for the enhancement of elastography through increased spatial resolution, providing a tangible benefit for the diagnosis of various diseases.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody proofs of the proposition TRUE, utilizing the standard set of transformation rules. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each rule within this framework is identically equivalent to a specific imperative algorithm. By incorporating the imperative algorithms as a subset of pseudorules, we maintain consistency with the original spirit of the concept of pseudorules as presented by Mints. This connection between algorithms and proofs offers a higher-level understanding of the imperative algorithms and the original problem statements they aim to solve, which can be reflected in the proofs themselves. This perspective on imperative algorithms as embedded within proofs is not dependent on any specific programming paradigm.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. By leveraging a scaling factor of $\left(1+\epsilon\right)$ for the distance metric, we can further optimize storage to a lower bound of $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

At very high-energy particle colliders like future muon colliders, multiple high-energy photons will likely be produced in the same interaction volume due to the small electromagnetic coupling. As a result, the relationship between the observed number of photons and the underlying photon production will be heavily affected by radiative effects, particularly in experiments that rely on precise photon measurements, such as Higgs boson or supersymmetry searches via the Higgs branch. In the context of QCD, we investigate the validity of the "leading logarithmic accuracy" in the "Strong Coupling" sector, which includes the collision by itself and additional "strongly coupled" photon collisions via the "photon-radiation of the collider," and find that this approximation is insufficient, specifically in the "photon-radiation of the collider" component, particularly in the "large-$N_\text{c}$" limit where $N_\text{c}$ is the number of color degrees of freedom. In contrast, we show that the "effective vector boson approximation" (EVA) yields more accurate results in the "strong coupling" sector of the theory. The effective vector boson approximation treats each individual photon production process as if it were an independent "collision," taking into account the effects of multiple photon production in the same interaction volume. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, we find that using a single
learned dynamics model for multiple tasks often leads to undesirable side
effects, a phenomenon we term "catastrophic intertask interference." To
mitigate this phenomenon, we propose two methods: first, we develop a way to
use partially isolated dynamics models; second, we design a more effective way
to share dynamics models using the concept of product of experts. Through our
experiments on various multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, we find our
proposed methods to be highly effective in reducing intertask interference.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

To break through the 64-kilohertz sound generation barrier for real-time speech synthesis, we've developed the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) model. This novel architecture, a variant of the WaveNet generator, incorporates two unique features. Firstly, we've divided the model into two frequency domains - one for low-frequency pitch-related information and the other for high-frequency timbre-related information - utilizing two separate sets of dilated convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) with different period lengths. Secondly, we've introduced a dynamic period length (DPL) for the DCNNs based on the spectral acoustic features, which allows the model to adapt to different period lengths for different frequency domains. The experimental results show that the QPNet model achieves a lower word error rate (WER) of 3.4% for the Librispeech test set and a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.25 for the 4-kilohertz sound quality evaluation.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), particularly in regards to its relation to the trace in the category of matrices. Through the integration of a scalar within the theory of shadows, a scalar-valued version of shadows is established as equivalent to the functors that extend THH, and it is demonstrated that this scalar-valued version of shadows coincides with the scalar multiple of the trace in the category of matrices. This finding provides a new perspective on a previously established result by the authors, and it also offers a more unified explanation for the properties and behavior of the THH of the circle.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate as its fundamental tool. Additionally, we outline a numerical strategy based on an iterative regularization approach to solve the inverse problem.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire canonical thermal ensemble along with the associated metaplectic group of operator equivalences.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, we investigate the relationship between the lightest dark matter state and the neutrino sector's properties, focusing on the phenomenon of WIMP dark matter. By integrating the simplest scoto-seesaw model into the standard model, we apply its parameters to WIMP dark matter theoretical predictions, using experimental constraints and theoretical requirements to limit parameter sets. Consequently, we derive guidelines for the simplest scoto-seesaw model's necessary features to ensure the stability of the Higgs vacuum and sufficient dark matter density.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
